etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English creken, criken, metathesis of Old English cearcian (“to chatter, creak, crash, gnash”), from Proto-West Germanic *krakōn (“to crash, crack, creak”), from Proto-Germanic *krakōną, from Proto-Indo-European *gerh₂- (“to make a sound, cry hoarsely”), ultimately of imitative origin.

Compare also Old English crǣccettan, crācettan (“to croak”), Albanian grykë (“throat”). More at crack.

definitions.definition: The sound produced by anything that creaks; a creaking.
(intransitive) To make a prolonged sharp grating or squeaking sound, as by the friction of hard substances.

quote.citation: 1856, Eleanor Marx-Aveling (translator), Gustave Flaubert (author), Madame Bovary, Part III, Chapter 10:
quote.text: Then when the four ropes were arranged the coffin was placed upon them. He watched it descend; it seemed descending for ever. At last a thud was heard; the ropes creaked as they were drawn up.

quote.citation: 1901, W. W. Jacobs, The Monkey's Paw:
quote.text: He heard the creaking of the bolt as it came slowly back, and at the same moment he found the monkey's paw, and frantically breathed his third and last wish.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To produce a creaking sound with.

quote.citation: c. 1604–1605 (date written), William Shakespeare, “All’s Well, that Ends Well”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:
quote.text: Creaking my shoes on the plain masonry.

quote.citation: 1941, Theodore Roethke, “On the Road to Woodlawn”, in Open House; republished in The Collected Poems of Theodore Roethke, 1975, →ISBN, page 21:
quote.text: I miss the polished brass, the powerful black horses,The drivers creaking the seats of the baroque hearses,  […]

definitions.definition: (intransitive, figurative) To suffer from strain or old age.

quote.citation: 2002, Stanley Wells, Shakespeare Survey, volume 39, page 205:
quote.text: Fascinating though this high-minded re-reading was, certain crucial joints of the play creaked a good deal under the strain.

quote.citation: 2007, Francis Pryor, Britain in the Middle Ages: An Archaeological History, page 232:
quote.text: The whole basis of feudalism, especially in the more intensively farmed champion arable landscapes of the Midlands, was starting to creak.
